top_choice_rationale: P001 (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn, B005) does best on my common test. It changed what can be credibly known, because random-coefficients demand with endogenous prices made substitution patterns, markups and merger effects measurable from market data. It has about three decades of use in merger review, regulation and applied work, so lasting influence is observed rather than predicted. Its credit core is a jointly authored contribution, which a citation limited to demand and competition in differentiated-product markets can match to the three names. It also faces no prior-prize overlap objection from any member. The reservations are real: it is a methods prize, estimates are sensitive to instruments and functional form, and Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are excluded by the three-name cap. I weigh them below its validated use and clean attribution. I rank P002 (Autor, Hanson, Dorn, B030) second. It is a substantive, design-based contribution with a clean trio, but persistence, magnitude and shift-share identification are still debated, and adjacency to recent prizes is contested. It is still a meritorious award, so I place it above no award. Support counts played no role in this ordering. I have not verified claims about replication records or prior prizes independently.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile for the credited names on P001 (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn) or P002 (Autor, Hanson, Dorn). I disclose that I am secretary and a long-term co-author of committee members Hassler (chair) and Boppart, who supported other configurations earlier. Their agreement or disagreement with me should not be read as independent confirmation. My field of technological change and inequality is topically adjacent to P002, but none of my listed co-authors are among its credited names. I record these ties without adjudicating them.
